GRADE 2 · DIAMOND / EARTH & LIGHT

A diamond's story.

How can a stone hold a flash of light?

FOUR LITTLE WONDERS

Where shall we look?

Grown-up beside you. A question is enough.

LOOK TOGETHER · 01

How could a diamond begin where sunlight cannot reach?

Find the tiny landscape at the top. How far below it is the pale crystal? What might the inward arrows mean?

A little explanation & something to try

Natural diamonds grow from carbon deep underground, where it is very hot and the pressure is enormous. The arrows stand for that squeeze. Their story stretches far back in Earth's past.

Try together. Trace from the painted tree down to the crystal. Imagine all the rock above it. This model cannot show the real distance.

LOOK TOGETHER · 02

What could something so tiny be made of?

Look at the small stone, then the big model. Follow a rod from one ball to the next. Where could the pattern keep going?

A little explanation & something to try

A diamond is made of carbon atoms, too small for our eyes to see. They join in a repeating pattern. The balls and rods help us picture it; a diamond does not contain little wooden sticks.

Try together. Choose one ball in the picture. Trace a connection to a neighbor, then another. Say one thing this model helps you imagine.

LOOK TOGETHER · 03

Does hard mean nothing can hurt it?

Compare the two surface drawings in the notebook. Which looks scratched? Find the numbers beside the minerals.

A little explanation & something to try

Hardness tells us how well a mineral resists scratches. Diamond is number 10 on the Mohs scale; talc is number 1. But a diamond can still chip or break. Hard does not mean unbreakable.

Try together. Draw a smooth patch and a scratched patch on paper. Tell each other what changed. We can explore the idea without scratching any real objects.

LOOK TOGETHER · 04

Where does the sparkle come from?

Start at the lamp. Follow the orange path into the model and back out. Where does its direction change?

A little explanation & something to try

Light can bend as it enters a diamond and bounce inside it. Carefully cut, flat faces help send light back toward our eyes. As the stone, light, or viewer moves, bright flashes appear and disappear.

Try together. Trace the painted light path in the air. Imagine the lamp going dark. Would the diamond make its own light?

Let the pictures lead you on.

A STORY TO OPEN TOGETHER

A diamond's story.

A stone. A flash. A question to follow together.

One little page at a time.

A beginning below

Before the sparkle

Little Wonderer peers at the deep rock. “No sunshine down there!” Long ago, far below the ground, heat and enormous pressure helped carbon grow into a diamond crystal. Its beginning took a long time.

What might the arrows be showing?

A hidden pattern

Too small to see

At the next table, a model towers over the stone. Its balls stand for tiny carbon atoms. “Neighbors!” says Little Wonderer. Strong connections hold them in a repeating pattern. A diamond keeps that pattern inside.

Follow a connection with your finger.

Carried toward daylight

An old journey

“Then how did it get up here?” Little Wonderer follows an arrow. Long after diamonds formed, some volcanic eruptions carried them upward in rising rock. Big Wonderer traces the path beside Little's finger.

Which came first: growing deep down or traveling up?

Hard, and still worth care

A different kind of strong

The next label says 10. Diamond sits at the top of the Mohs scratch scale. “Nothing can hurt it?” Little asks. “It can still chip,” says Big Wonderer. Hard to scratch does not mean impossible to break.

What did Little's first idea leave out?

A path for light

The light comes along

A lamp shines on the cut-diamond model. Light bends as it enters, bounces inside, and comes out again. The flat, cut faces guide its path. Little Wonderer follows the orange line. “The light came from somewhere else!”

Trace from the lamp to the way out.

Something to look at again

One more look

Little shifts sideways. One face dims; another catches the light. Together, they sketch two places to look from. “What if the light moved?” Little asks. Big Wonderer leaves room for the question.

Keep that question, or tell each other your own.

For grown-ups & print downloads

Wonder first; explanations can wait. These museum scenes are imagined models, not photographs. Earth layers, atom connections, ray angles, and diamond sizes are simplified. We focus on natural diamonds: carbon crystallizes under deep-Earth heat and pressure, and later eruptions can carry it upward. A diamond's age is not a stopwatch for its growth; growth histories vary. The model balls represent carbon atoms, whose strong repeating connections help explain hardness. Mohs 10 ranks scratch resistance, not toughness or a tenfold amount. Diamonds can chip or break. Bending light is refraction; bouncing light is reflection. A skilled cutter makes facets that direct light; a rough crystal need not look like a cut diamond. Some light escapes in other directions; the orange line shows just one simplified path. Keep the scientific words optional. All activities can happen with pictures, talk, and drawing. No real diamonds, scratch tests, or tools are needed. Pause whenever you have had enough.

About 15 min: choose a wonder, read the six short moments, then revisit a picture. Read aloud for Leo; pointing, talking, and pausing all count. Let the question come before the explanation.
